1:
Delitzsch states the principle that makes the whole register readable. The list begins with the sheep gate and the stretch of wall beside it, built by the priests, and ends with the goldsmiths and merchants building up to that same gate; and since it is said almost without exception that each party built at the hand of, next to, the party named before, the course of the wall is being followed throughout, and the gates are named in the order they actually stood. The chapter is a circuit, not a catalogue.

That the high priest opens it is noticed by everyone and pressed by three. Gill identifies Eliashib as the grandson of Jeshua, his father Joiakim, and observes that in rising first he set an example to priests and people alike. Wesley makes the same identification and turns it into a rule: ministers should be foremost in every good work, animating others by their example as well as their doctrine. Henry says it more sharply still — if there be labour in it, who so fit as they to work; if danger, who so fit as they to venture.

Why the priests took that gate in particular is answered from its use. Henry points out that it was called the sheep gate because the sheep for sacrifice were brought through it, so the priests undertook it because the offerings of the Lord made by fire were their inheritance. Ellicott adds the detail of the victims being washed in the neighbouring pool before passing through.

The harder question is the word sanctified, said of this gate and of no other. Wesley faces the alternative squarely: the word can sometimes mean prepared or repaired, and on that reading nothing ceremonial happened at all. He rejects it, on two grounds — that the consecrating sense is the commoner one, and that the word is used here alone, which a merely technical meaning would not explain. Henry offers three reasons for the ceremony without choosing between them: because the gate led to the temple; because the building began there and was probably finished first, so that the city and its walls were solemnly committed to divine protection at that point; or because the priests were its builders, and men set apart to God should sanctify what they do. Clarke gives a fourth and narrower one, that as sacrifice had begun as soon as an altar was built, the gate by which the sacrifices entered ought to be set apart for that use and no other. Ellicott looks forward instead of back, taking the act as an earnest of the consecration of the whole wall later on.

On the phrase that carries the reader round the circuit, Ellicott observes that at his hand is the customary formula of the chapter and that it does honour to the high priest where it first appears, since Eliashib must be supposed to have presided over the religious ceremonial only. Delitzsch works at its grammar, noting that the singular suffix first covers Eliashib and all the priests, so that a company is treated now as a plural and now as a single agent; and he places the stretch built by the men of Jericho and by Zaccur between the corner tower and the fish gate in the north wall.

Two observations close the opening. Gill notes that the men of Jericho were the descendants of that city's former inhabitants and began exactly where the priests left off. Henry makes more of their presence: many who worked here were not inhabitants of Jerusalem at all and so consulted purely the public welfare, with the men of Jericho among the first of them. His conclusion is the one the chapter keeps proving — that united force will carry what no individual dares venture on, and many hands make light work.
3:
Where the fish gate stood, and which fish came through it, is a genuine three-way disagreement. Gill canvasses the options and comes down westward: Lightfoot puts it south, others north, and some make it the road to the sea of Galilee and the Jordan and the whole east and north country, but Gill judges it most likely to have faced west toward the Mediterranean, Tyre and Joppa, whence the fish were brought. He cites Rauwolff for a gate still standing on that side behind Mount Zion, called the gate of Hebron because the Hebron road ran through it. Ellicott takes the opposite view in a line, saying the fish entered through it from the Jordan and Galilee. Delitzsch agrees with neither on the trade and with Thenius on nothing: the name came from the fish market beside it, to which Syrians brought sea fish, and the gate stood not hard against the corner tower, as Thenius drew it in his plan, but somewhat west of it in the north wall, two lengths of wall having been built between the two.

Clarke declines the whole exercise, and his refusal is the sharpest sentence in the chapter. We really know scarcely anything about these gates, he says — what they were, why they were called by these names, or where in the wall they stood; all plans of Jerusalem, its temple, walls and gates are mere works of conjecture. What he cannot forgive is the confidence: and yet, he adds, how learnedly have some men written on all these subjects.

The ironwork of the gates is handled more soberly. Delitzsch notes that the two terms after the doors both denote bars for closing them, while Ellicott separates the pair — the one word meaning the crossbars and the other the catches that hold them at either end — and says the same distinction runs through several later verses.

A technical distinction then enters the register and governs the rest of it. Gill observes that where the text turns from built to repaired, the change is exact: that part of the wall had not been wholly demolished but only weakened, so the work was strengthening rather than rebuilding, and the word is used in that sense all the way through what follows. Ellicott confirms it from the Hebrew, which says literally strengthened where it had earlier said built. Delitzsch glosses the verb the same way, as repairing the gaps and holes in the wall, and picks out two of the men named: Meremoth, who took a second portion further round, and Meshullam, whom the book elsewhere shows to have been a person of consideration in the city.

The one refusal in the chapter is recorded without softening. Ellicott calls the verse remarkable on two counts — that it introduces men of Tekoa who are not among those who returned with Zerubbabel, and that it terms the common labour the work of their Lord — and notes that these furnish the solitary instance of internal opposition to the building, while the ordinary people of the place went on to do double duty. Delitzsch explains the idiom exactly: to bring the neck to the service is to bring it under the yoke, to put oneself under another's service, and it is that submission the nobles would not make. Wesley guesses at the motive and allows three — sloth, covetousness, or a secret compliance with the enemies of the Jews — and then delivers the verdict the text itself implies, that they are branded to all posterity for it. His closing question is put to nobility in general: what is their rank good for, if not that it places them in a higher and larger sphere of usefulness?
6:
The old gate is named nowhere else in scripture, and the identifications multiply accordingly. Gill lists four: that it took its name from the old city of Salem; that Lightfoot equates it with one of the gates numbered earlier; that Vatablus makes it the gate of the old pool; or, as Gill himself rather prefers, that it was the gate of the old wall which Josephus mentions, opening toward the north of the land. Ellicott offers a fifth, that it was probably the gate later called of Damascus, and notes that the reading gate of the old wall, which several have adopted, rests on a conjectural addition to the text and treats the phrase as set against the broad wall further on.

The throne of the governor divides the witnesses more sharply, because it is not agreed what kind of thing the phrase is. Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all take it as a landmark: the residence of the Persian governor of the province beyond the river, where he lodged and gave judgment when he came to Jerusalem. Clarke adds the historical change that followed, that before Nehemiah the city was ruled by a deputy of the Persian king and afterwards by governors and judges chosen from among the people themselves. Delitzsch reports the words as questionable and gives the alternative construction, followed by Bertheau and others, under which they do not mark a point on the wall at all but describe the builders — men of Gibeon and Mizpah belonging to the governor's seat. On that reading the verse is quietly recording something significant, that Jews outside Nehemiah's own jurisdiction came and worked on the wall.

The tradesmen are treated as guilds rather than individuals. Gill, following Jarchi, takes the goldsmiths for a family named from their trade. Delitzsch reads the plural as apposition, Uzziel standing for himself and the fellow-craftsmen working under his direction, and Hananiah described as a son of the apothecaries because he belonged to that guild. Clarke confirms the guild structure, observing that from the remotest period the nation had artists in the elegant and ornamental trades and that by this date goldsmiths, apothecaries and merchants were formed into companies; and he narrows the second name, which he would rather render as dealers in drugs, aromatics and spices, for embalming or for supplying the temple with its incense.

One clause in the same verse is genuinely obscure, and both close readers say so. Delitzsch notes that the words have been variously interpreted and settles what the broad wall was — a named stretch running between the tower of the furnaces and the gate of Ephraim, not simply a place that happened to be wide, as Bertheau would have it. Ellicott goes after the verb. The word rendered fortified means literally left, and he takes that sense: the builders left Jerusalem untouched as far as the stretch of wall that needed no restoration extended. What he draws from it is an argument from silence with some force — the gate of Ephraim stood in that stretch, and the chapter says nothing whatever about rebuilding so important a gate. Wesley notices the same oddity of wording without resolving it, only that the text does not say they repaired but that they fortified.

Finally, the rulers of half parts. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all understand the city itself to have been divided, one portion falling to Judah and the other to Benjamin, each with its own governor; Clarke names Rephaiah and Shallum as the pair, and Wesley compares the division into regions at Rome, placing the Benjamite half nearer the temple. Delitzsch and Ellicott both read it the other way: what was halved was not the city but the district of country belonging to it, and Delitzsch supports this from a later verse where a town and its district are expressly distinguished.
10:
Working opposite one's own front door recurs through the register, and two readings of it are on offer. Gill takes it as sensible self-interest: the man could hardly object to that stretch, and might be expected to repair it well and strongly, since his own safety depended on it. Clarke suspects something less voluntary — that some of the principal people were obliged to repair the wall facing their own dwellings, and that this may have been the general rule rather than a happy coincidence.

The phrase rendered the other piece raises a real textual question, and the two close readers come down on opposite sides. Delitzsch sets out the case made by Bertheau: a second measure implies a first, and in several places the same builders are indeed named twice, so where a second portion is credited to men who have not been mentioned before, something has dropped out. Bertheau infers from this that the text has not come down to us complete, and thinks it likely that statements about the gate of Ephraim and its neighbourhood once stood earlier in the chapter. Ellicott declines the inference. The expression does occur where an earlier portion has been named, he grants, but it occurs several times where none has; and in those places it need mean no more than the margin says, a second measure reckoned against what has just been described. On his reading nothing is missing and nothing needs restoring.

One of the names carries a story. Gill reports from Ben Melech that Hallohesh was so called either from being an enchanter of serpents or from being a wise and prudent counsellor, the word admitting both. Clarke passes on the same conjecture in its first form only, the son of the Enchanter, named from an art of charming serpents.

The daughters who worked beside Shallum are the most disputed detail in the chapter, because it is not agreed that they were daughters at all. The alternative is grammatical: in Hebrew the villages dependent on a town are its daughters, and Shallum is named here as ruler of a district, so the clause could be recording that his villages turned out with him. Delitzsch rules it out on the pronoun, which he says can only refer to Shallum himself and not to the district. Ellicott knows the suggestion and calls it needless, giving a reason that is social rather than grammatical: the women of Jerusalem might well do voluntarily what nobody would have pressed them, as women, to do.

What the daughters actually did is then left open. Wesley supposes them heiresses or rich widows. Henry takes the same view and draws the consequence, that they were not capable of personal service on the wall but had their portions in their own hands, and so contributed money for materials and wages; and he sets them beside the women whom Paul describes as having laboured with him in the gospel. Delitzsch, for his part, is content to leave them at the wall without saying what their share of the work was.

Two smaller notes close the section. Gill observes that the fathers of Malchijah and Hashub were heads of families who had come up out of the captivity with Zerubbabel, and Delitzsch confirms both houses from the earlier register of the return. It is a quiet point but a recurring one in this chapter: a good many of the men repairing the wall are named elsewhere as belonging to families who had already made the journey back.
13:
Delitzsch places the valley gate in the west, close to where the Jaffa gate now stands, and quotes Tobler for the judgment that on that ridge near the present citadel there must almost always have been an entrance provided with gates. He also explains why two names are joined: Hanun was probably the chief of the men of Zanoah, which he locates as the modern Zanna in the wady west of Jerusalem. Clarke adds only that Zanoah was a town of Judah.

The thousand cubits are read as a measure of damage rather than of labour. Ellicott points out that the verb here is not built but strengthened, and infers that this comparatively large stretch, given in round numbers, had suffered less than the rest and needed correspondingly less doing to it. Delitzsch keeps the clause governed by the main verb of the verse and rejects Bertheau's attempt to detach it.

Whether one of the builders was a Rechabite is raised and then doubted. Gill takes the possibility seriously enough to meet the objection: the Rechabites were forbidden to build houses, but perhaps a man who might not build a private dwelling for himself could still be employed on walls and fortresses for the public safety. Having made the case he abandons it, thinking it more probable that this Malchiah was not of that family at all. Ellicott settles it on the article: the text says the son of Rechab, not a son of Rechab, so the phrase is a patronymic and not a claim of descent from the order.

Beth-haccerem produces the same split that half part of Jerusalem produced earlier. Clarke treats it as a village or town; Ellicott as the district around that place; Wesley as a town or territory whose government was divided between two men. The disagreement is the same one throughout the chapter, whether these rulers governed places or the country belonging to them.

At the fountain gate a verb appears that occurs nowhere else in the list. Delitzsch derives it from a root meaning to shade or cover and takes it as the equivalent of the laying of beams mentioned at the earlier gates, probably a covering of beams laid across. Ellicott glosses it the same way. Between them the two readings agree that the gate received a roof of some kind, which the other gates are not said to have had.

The last stretch of this section is the one the topographers care about most, and it is also where they begin to lose the thread. Ellicott identifies the pool of Siloah with the pool called earlier the king's pool, which was fed through a long subterranean conduit and watered the royal gardens, the name itself carrying the sense of water sent. Clarke is content to say it is probably the pool the evangelists mention. The stairs going down from the city of David, Ellicott places on the steep side of Ophel and reports that traces of them are thought still to survive. Clarke explains why such stairs were needed at all: Jerusalem was built on very uneven ground, with hills taken inside the walls, so that steps were necessary in different places — much, he says, as one sees in the city of Bristol. And then Ellicott admits the difficulty that governs the rest of the chapter: from this point it becomes very hard to trace the exact course of the wall.
16:
Delitzsch notices that the register changes its formula at this point. Where the earlier entries said at his hand, from here on they mostly say after him, the older phrase surviving only twice more. The stretch now described runs to a point opposite the sepulchres of David, then to the pool that was made, and then to the house of the mighty.

On the first of those landmarks the two topographers contradict each other flatly. Delitzsch takes the sepulchres to be the burial place of the house of David within the city of David, and puts the wall opposite them on the eastern side of Zion, where Thenius has argued there was an entrance to the royal tomb. Ellicott places them on the western side of the Temple instead, and adds the concession that undercuts everyone: they have never yet been traced.

The other two landmarks draw a rare measure of agreement. Clarke passes on Calmet's suggestion that the pool that was made was the reservoir Hezekiah constructed during the siege by Sennacherib, and Ellicott independently offers the same identification. On the house of the mighty they differ only in rank: Clarke supposes a post where a band of soldiers was kept, or the city guard, while Ellicott makes it the barracks of David's own picked troops. Gill supplies what the verse leaves out about the builder rather than the building, that Beth-zur was a strong fortified place in Judah.

Ellicott marks the progress of the circuit when the Levites appear: the wall is now coming round toward the Temple, which is why the Temple's own servants take up the work here. He reads Rehum as the man under whom the Levites served as a body, and explains the awkward phrase in his part by pointing to the next verse, where the other half of the same district is accounted for.

Who the brethren of that next verse were is disputed, and the disagreement is small but real. Delitzsch takes them to be the inhabitants of the second half-district, the men under Bavai, so that the word means simply the other half of the same population. Gill offers two possibilities without settling between them: either the brethren of the two men just named, or, as Jarchi has it, the Levites in general as a body of brethren. The choice decides whether the verse is naming a district or an order.

What the section shows, taken together, is how much of this chapter's geography rests on inference. Two of its three landmarks here are identified only by a supposition — Calmet's for the pool, a guess at a garrison for the house of the mighty — and the third, the royal sepulchres, is placed on opposite sides of the city by the two men best qualified to place it, with one of them admitting that nobody has ever found it. The register is precise about who built; it is the ground under the names that has gone.
19:
The armoury at the turning of the wall is described confidently by everyone and located consistently by nobody. Delitzsch treats the word as an abbreviation of house of arms and then declines to be precise, saying the place cannot be more exactly stated: probably on the east side of Zion where the city wall formed an angle, or else occupying an angle within the city itself with no buildings adjoining it southward. He rejects Bertheau's attempt to fix it at a tower Tobler describes midway between the modern Zion gate and the dung gate. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as the armoury of the corner and puts it at the north-west corner of the city of David, with its own separate wall — the opposite side of the city from Delitzsch's guess. Clarke keeps to what it was rather than where: either a tower defending the angle where two walls met, or the city arsenal, where shields and spears were kept to arm the people in a time of danger.

Then comes the one adverb in the chapter, and it divides the witnesses more sharply than any landmark. Gill takes it at the root: the word signifies anger, and he has Baruch angry — with himself or with others — that any backwardness had been shown to the work, and therefore attending to it with all the haste and eagerness imaginable. Delitzsch denies that sense outright. The word cannot here mean to be angry or incensed, he says, but is to be taken as emulate or contend, with the perfect subordinated adverbially to the verb that follows; so what is recorded is not temper but competition. Ellicott reads it as emulation too, and then registers what he cannot explain: the reason for this man's emulation in building next to the high priest's house does not appear. Clarke and Henry keep the plain sense of zeal without the edge of either anger or rivalry — Clarke that he distinguished himself by his activity, Henry that he worked with an inflamed zeal, not because the others were cold or indifferent but because he was the most vigorous of them and so made himself remarkable, probably provoking the rest to make more haste.

The same clause has attracted a conjectural emendation, which Delitzsch reports and refuses. Bertheau would read the consonants as up the hill rather than earnestly, on the argument that the verb everywhere else in this description stands without such a qualifier. Delitzsch turns that argument round: throughout the whole narrative, definitions of place follow the verb and never precede it, so a locality standing where this word stands would be the anomaly, not the adverb.

The section ends with a man taking a second turn. Gill notes that Meremoth had already worked on another part of the wall and, having finished it, set his hand to the work again; Ellicott says the same, that he added this stretch under the high priest's house to his earlier labour. Henry gathers the pattern that Meremoth belongs to — those who had finished helped their fellows and took another share where the need was greatest — and points out that the men of Tekoa did the same, which is the more striking because their own nobles had set them the opposite example. Wesley, characteristically, gets something out of a preposition: since the wall is measured first to the door of the high priest's house and then to the end of it, the door cannot have stood in the middle of the house, as doors commonly do now, but at one end.
22:
Where the priests of the plain lived is a straight disagreement about one Hebrew word. Ellicott takes the plain for the Jordan valley, the Kikkar of scripture, and Delitzsch argues the point at length: the word does not, as Bertheau inferred, mean the open country round Jerusalem, but the Jordan valley, so that the verse is quietly telling us priests were then living down there, probably near Jericho. Clarke reads it the other way, noting that some of the temple officers and particularly the singers dwelt in the plain country round about the city and supposing that priests lived among them. Gill will not choose, offering the plain of Jericho, where a station of priests existed at least in later times, or else the plain about Jerusalem. Either way the men came in from outside to work on a wall they would not live behind.

Of the next builders nothing at all is known, and Delitzsch says so without embarrassment. Benjamin and Hashub repaired opposite their house, Azariah beside his, and the commentary has nothing to add: nothing further is known of these individuals. Gill adds only that Binnui began where Azariah left off, and that Palal, repairing over against the turning of the wall, lived at that spot and so worked on what stood right in front of him.

The tower at the prison court raises a small grammatical question with a real consequence. The Hebrew allows the word high to be attached either to the tower or to the king's house, and Delitzsch attaches it to the tower. His reason is that nothing whatever is known of an upper and a lower royal house, so the phrase king's upper house would be describing a distinction that does not exist. He grants it would be more natural, with Bertheau, to suppose an upper and a lower tower at the prison court, but denies that the word implies any such pair: it means first of all high, elevated, and needs no lower counterpart. What settles it for him is that the very same tower is called the great tower a few verses later, which suits high rather than upper. Ellicott renders it the same way without arguing the case, as the high tower outlying from the king's palace, and supplies the domestic detail that makes the prison court intelligible — a palace generally had its prison, and the gate named after it stood close by.

On the corner the two agree as far as the word and then part on the map. Ellicott fixes it as the north-eastern angle of the city of David. Delitzsch is content to call it the angle and the corner without naming a compass point, which is consistent with his practice through this stretch: he will state what the Hebrew says and decline to place it when the ground cannot bear the weight.
26:
The note about the Nethinim produces two disagreements at once, and both are sharp. Gill takes Ophel for a high tower standing on the wall at this point, and reads the verse as recording that the temple servants repaired here because this was where they lived. Ellicott takes Ophel for the long rounded spur of ground running south of the Temple, on whose sides the temple servants still dwelt, kept separate from others, occupying a tract that reached from the water gate on the east to the outlying tower of the king's citadel on the west. And he draws the opposite conclusion from the verse: nothing at all is said about their part in the general labour. On one reading the Nethinim are builders; on the other the verse is a parenthesis about where they lived, inserted because the wall had reached their quarter — which is how Delitzsch takes it too, calling it a remark set into the description at the point where the wall begins to enclose Ophel. Ellicott adds that some have proposed inserting who before dwelt, following the Syriac, and judges the addition unnecessary.

Delitzsch then works on the eastern landmarks. The water gate toward the east he places beyond the south-eastern corner of the temple area, and reports Bertheau's rival placing on the east side near the golden gate, which rests on identifying the open space where Ezra read to the people with the open place before that gate. For the wall of Ophel itself he supplies the building history: Jotham had built much on it, and Manasseh afterwards carried a very high wall round its western, southern and eastern sides — no wall being needed on the north, where the southern wall of the temple area already protected it.

The men of Tekoa then reappear, and everyone notices. Gill observes that having finished the piece they undertook earlier they took on this one as well, which shows their zeal and diligence the more plainly because their own nobles had been so backward and had withdrawn from the work altogether. Wesley makes the same connection, that they dispatched their first share sooner than others did theirs. Ellicott, reading the text rather than the men, points out that the plural after them is literally after him, and refers it back to the last individual named.

Delitzsch explains how two quite different stretches of wall can both be described as opposite the great tower: the tower stood well inside the city wall, so the length running north along the eastern ridge and the length running east from the corner could each be said to face it. The piece here recorded he traces along the Tyropoeon valley as far as the wall of Ophel.

The horse gate closes the section, and it is named from its traffic rather than its position. Gill offers three explanations and prefers none: stables near it, horses led through it to be watered at the brook nearby, or horses taken out to be exercised in the valley; he adds that Josephus mentions a horse tower that may have stood close by. Clarke keeps to the watering and places the gate near the temple. Delitzsch tries to fix it and shows how difficult that is: the older histories put it not far from the temple and the palace, while this chapter puts it next to the wall of Ophel, so with Thenius he looks for it in the wall crossing the Tyropoeon valley, about where the dung gate now stands — against Bertheau, who argues from the prophet for a site on the western side of the Kidron valley below the eastern corner of the temple area. On one small point Delitzsch is firm: the phrase from above does not mean a point to the north of the gate.
29:
The keeper of the east gate is identified two different ways. Ellicott takes him for the man of that name who appears among the descendants of David in the older genealogy. Delitzsch says he can hardly be that man, rejects a second candidate whose family guarded the south side of the temple, and leaves the identification open. On the gate itself Delitzsch is firm: the east gate is undoubtedly the east gate of the temple and is not, as Bertheau would have it, the water gate toward the east named earlier. He is equally firm about what does not follow from the office — that because Shemaiah kept that gate, he and his under-keepers must have fortified it. The text does not say where he repaired, and Delitzsch will not supply it.

The sixth son of Zalaph is the detail this chapter is remembered for. Gill states the arithmetic plainly, that the man had six sons and only the youngest worked here, recorded to his great commendation. Wesley draws the inference the text invites — the five elder brethren laid not their hands to the work — and turns it into a maxim: in doing what is good we need not wait to see our betters go before us. Henry presses it further still, that the younger brother who does God and his generation the better service is the better gentleman, since those are most honourable who are most useful.

One builder had no house to repair in front of. Henry notices that the man who worked over against his chamber was likely only a lodger, and takes that as the point: if a man who has but a chamber will repair before that, he has done his part. Delitzsch works on the word rather than the man, observing that it occurs only here and twice elsewhere, and that in one of those places it seems to mean a dwelling.

The last stretch is the most obscurely worded in the chapter, and the witnesses divide over how to cut the sentence. Delitzsch sets out both: the Masoretic pointing makes Malchiah repair as far as the house of the Nethinim and the merchants, opposite the gate Miphkad and to the upper chamber of the corner, while the Greek divides the words differently, so that Malchiah goes as far as the house of the Nethinim and the spice-merchants repair the stretch facing the gate. Bertheau prefers the Greek; Delitzsch thinks his grounds questionable. Ellicott reads the same clause as the house rather than the place, and guesses at why traders and temple servants are named together — the merchants who brought doves for the worshippers delivered them to the house of the Nethinim. Of the gate Miphkad he can say only that nothing is known about it.

The circuit closes where it opened. Gill notes simply that the building first began at the sheep gate and now ends there. Delitzsch draws out what the closure proves: the description begins and ends at the same gate and links its sections throughout by the same two phrases, good grounds for concluding that the forty-two sections and gates here particularized describe the entire fortified wall without a gap. He adds a reason why this last stretch needed least doing — the eastern wall of the temple area may have suffered less when the Chaldeans demolished the city, or have been partly repaired already when the temple was rebuilt. Clarke ends on the two trades, noting that the word rendered goldsmiths may mean workers in metal of any kind, that the naming of goldsmiths and merchants shows both were incorporated bodies by this date, and that the versions cannot agree what they were: the Syriac makes them goldsmiths and druggists, the Arabic smelters and porters, and the Greek copies divide between merchants and sellers of shields.
